newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Palestinians strained by Israel entry ban.
newsitem.headline: Palestinians strained by Israel entry ban.

text.p: Since two suicide bombers killed 13 people in a Jewish market four days ago Zuhair, 35, has been barred from Israel and out of work.
"I spent from my savings and I can continue this for a couple of days," said Zuhair, a Palestinian who supports his family of seven by laying tiles in Tel Aviv for $35 a day.
"But if I don't go back to my work soon, I don't know how I can manage," he told Reuters, declining to give his last name.

Israel closed its borders to the two million Palestinians of the West Bank and Gaza Strip immediately after Wednesday's bombing and restricted travel between Arab villages, cities and towns in the territories.
"Palestinians are under house arrest because of this double closure," said Shaher Saed, General-Secretary of the Palestine General Federation of Trade Unions.
"People are eating stored food. Someday we'll run out," said Fraij al-Khairy, Palestinian Deputy Minister of Civil Affairs.
Khairy said trade between the territories and Israel stopped after the bombing when Palestinians refused an offer to import Israeli goods without being allowed to export their own.
"This is the strictest closure ever since the Palestinian Authority took over... We are in a big and crucial prison. This closure is beyond the human imagination," he said.
Since the bombing, the Allenby Bridge, which links Jordan and the West Bank, has been closed to Palestinians as has been the crossing linking the Gaza Strip and Egypt.

Under interim peace deals between Israel and the Palestine Liberation Organisation (PLO) since September 1993, Israel remains in charge of international borders. The Palestinian Authority is in charge of self-rule enclaves set up in most of Gaza and parts of the West Bank under the deals.
Israel is also withholding tax refunds of $200 million it owes the authority.
"They'll be resumed like everything else when we see a change of attitude in the Palestinian Authority," said David Bar-Illan, communications chief for Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.
Israeli officials say the restrictions are necessary to prevent more suicide bomb attacks.
Palestinians say the closures and other steps are collective punishment.

"The idea is to exchange land for peace, not labour for peace. Every time there is a violent act, they put a ban on the workers," said Mohammed Shtayyeh, Director of the Palestinian Economic Council for Development and Reconstruction.

Since Israel and PLO signed their historic 1993 deal, as many as 60,000 Palestinians daily entered Israel legally to work. But periodic closures for security reasons have often kept them from work and played havoc with the Palestinian economy.
Normally, unemployment in the West Bank and Gaza ranges from 15 to 26 percent, but during closures it can jump to more than 60 percent, Palestinian analysts said.
They said the current restrictions could cost the Palestinian economy $6-7 million per day.
Even if the borders open relatively quickly, Palestinian workers may find they've been replaced by foreign workers.
Israel's Association of Contractors and Builders put a ban on hiring Palestinians after the bombing.
"We are not against the Palestinians, we are against the situation," said Amos Baram, head of the association.
"But of the 40,000 to 50,000 Palestinians entering each day to work...one might be one of them (a bomber). We can't take any more responsibility."
